intro: A dying woman dreams that she is dancing: Valse triste begins on a theatre stage, with Death among the guests. Judith Bokor’s 1925 recording gives its long melody to the cello, with piano accompaniment.

sections.label: A · A quiet waltz for two
sections.mNote: The cello sings over the piano’s three-beat accompaniment

sections.label: B · The waltz opens out
sections.mNote: Related waltz melodies pass between the dancing phrases

sections.label: A′ · The quieter dance returns
sections.mNote: The opening waltz returns with lighter accompaniment

sections.label: A″ · The waltz swells again
sections.mNote: Cello and piano gather the dance into longer phrases

sections.label: Coda · Three quiet chords
sections.mNote: The dance slows into its last short phrases

relations.label: The opening waltz returns quietly
relations.basis: The opening waltz links the contrasting waltzes and is recalled in the quieter central stretch of this cello-and-piano arrangement. That recurring role is described by Richard Dyer at https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste; the later excerpt lies in the withdrawal marked near 132 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.926, sustained 14 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 143 s (cache/form/sibelius-valse-triste.txt, candidate 4; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A waltz for two
cues.text: The piano marks three beats while the cello carries the longer melody across them. Sibelius begins with the bare rhythm of a waltz; the tune takes shape above it, slowly, as though the dancers are just finding their feet.
cues.evidence: Sibelius, Valse triste, Breitkopf & Härtel orchestral score, plate Part. B. 1853, p. 2: Lento, 3/4, accompaniment before the melody. Richard Dyer also describes this opening: https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste . This recording uses cello and piano.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Death at the masked ball
cues.text: In Arvid Järnefelt’s play Kuolema, an old woman dreams of a masked ball. Her partner turns out to be Death. Sibelius writes the music in 1903 for this play by his brother-in-law.
cues.evidence: Richard Dyer, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note, describes the scene, the family connection and the 1903 incidental music. https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste

cues.title: Four waltzes, one thread
cues.text: Sibelius joins four related waltzes. The opening dance keeps coming back between them, a hesitant thread through the longer melodies. In this arrangement, the cello carries that changing song while the piano keeps the steps beneath it.
cues.evidence: Richard Dyer identifies four related waltzes, linked by the opening waltz, in his Boston Symphony Orchestra note. The cue describes the piece’s design across the surrounding passage. https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: From theatre to concert hall
cues.text: On 25 April 1904, Sibelius conducts the concert première in Helsinki. The piece appears separately in print that year. Its first title is Valse lente — “Slow waltz” — before it becomes the “Sad waltz” known everywhere.
cues.evidence: Richard Dyer, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note: Helsinki concert première, 25 April 1904, separate publication in 1904 and original title Valse lente. https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste

cues.title: The last three chords
cues.text: The dance slows and the opening waltz returns in short phrases. Three quiet chords remain after the melody has finished. In the orchestral score, Sibelius leaves those chords to four solo violins; here the farewell belongs to cello and piano.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate Part. B. 1853, p. 11: Lento assai, followed by three pp chords for four solo violins. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/2d/IMSLP212006-SIBLEY1802.12357.ba00-39087008746275score.pdf . Richard Dyer describes the three-chord postlude at https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste .
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The waltz slows into three chords
transitions.how: Sibelius marks the closing passage Lento assai — very slow. Short phrases recall the opening dance, then the melody stops and three quiet chords close the piece. The cello-and-piano arrangement keeps this brief farewell after the waltz.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate Part. B. 1853, p. 11: Lento assai and three closing chords. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/2d/IMSLP212006-SIBLEY1802.12357.ba00-39087008746275score.pdf . The precise arrangement used by Bokor is unidentified.

composer.born: 8 December 1865, Hämeenlinna, Grand Duchy of Finland
composer.epithet: He watched sixteen swans circle over Ainola, gave their flight to the horns, and spent four years getting the Fifth Symphony right.
facts: Wegelius in Helsinki, 1885–89; Becker in Berlin; Fuchs and Goldmark in Vienna
Ainola, Lars Sonck’s timber house near Lake Tuusula, from 1904
Swedish at home; Finnish at school and in Kullervo and Luonnotar
Seven symphonies, one violin concerto, tone poems, theatre music, songs and chamber music
composer.background:
In Vienna in 1891, Sibelius auditioned for the Philharmonic and failed. He wanted to be a violinist; the jury found him too nervous even for an orchestral post. He was twenty-five, studying composition with Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark, spending money he did not have at parties and taking in as much music as the city could offer. After hearing Bruckner’s Third Symphony he thought its author the greatest living composer. Meanwhile, in his lodgings, he was studying the rhythms of the Finnish Kalevala.

He had been born in Hämeenlinna in 1865, when Finland was a grand duchy of the Russian Empire. His father, a doctor, died three years later, leaving debts. At home the family spoke Swedish; at school Janne learnt Finnish. He played chamber music with his sister Linda and brother Christian, and in 1885 went to Helsinki, nominally to study law. Martin Wegelius’s Music Institute soon claimed his days. There he befriended Ferruccio Busoni and worked through quartets by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. His professional name came cheaply: he found a dead uncle’s visiting cards. “Jean is now my musical name,” he told Uncle Pehr on 31 March 1886. Studies with Albert Becker in Berlin followed Helsinki, then came Vienna.
